overall_summary: The channel's highest-performing content heavily revolves around extreme space anomalies, bizarre exoplanets, and cosmic mysteries (e.g., TrES-2b, supersonic rubies, burning ice), which consistently generate 300 to 1,000+ views. Conversely, psychological and brain-related facts (e.g., fake memories, songs stuck in head) struggle to gain traction, often stalling under 100 views. Transitioning to slightly longer durations (18-21s) for space topics has also shown a positive correlation with higher engagement and likes.

winning_patterns.evidence: The Planet of Burning Ice (1,055 views), The Planet Darker Than Coal (1,014 views), and This Planet Rains Supersonic Rubies (721 views) represent the channel's top tier of performance and engagement.
winning_patterns.action: Double down on extreme space environments, focusing on mind-bending physical properties, strange rains, and unique exoplanets, utilizing high-contrast cosmic visuals.

weak_patterns.evidence: Multiple uploads of 'Your Brain Can Create Fake Memories' yielded only 5, 11, and 53 views, while 'The Real Reason Songs Get Stuck In Your Head' stalled at 17 views.
weak_patterns.action: Phase out soft psychology and cognitive tricks unless they can be framed through a highly dramatic, cinematic, or historical lens.

next_video.concept: The planet where it rains liquid iron and has winds faster than sound.
next_video.opening_direction: Start with a high-contrast, cinematic visual of a planet engulfed in dark red shadows, captioned: 'This planet is so hot, it literally rains liquid metal...'
next_video.twist_direction: Reveal that the winds are so violent they blow this molten iron rain sideways at 5,000 miles per hour, turning the entire atmosphere into a flying shredder.
next_video.reason: Aligns with the highly successful exoplanet theme (TrES-2b and Supersonic Rubies) which drives the highest views and engagement on the channel.

experiment: Test a 21-second cinematic micro-story format about a real historical space mystery (e.g., the 'Wow! Signal' or the lost cosmonauts) to bridge the gap between space facts and cinematic storytelling.
